title: Photosynthesis in Plants
subject: Science
confidenceNotes: Equation and main labels are clear.
Teacher should confirm the cropped output label before sharing.
objective: Students explain photosynthesis as the process by which green plants make glucose using sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, and chlorophyll.
keyConcepts: Green plants are producers because they can make their own food.
Leaves are the main site of photosynthesis because they contain chlorophyll.
Roots absorb water from soil and carry it to leaves through the stem.
Carbon dioxide enters leaves through tiny openings called stomata.
Sunlight provides the energy needed to change raw materials into glucose.
Oxygen is released as a useful by-product during photosynthesis.
Glucose can be used immediately for energy or stored as starch.
teachingScript:
Begin by asking students where a plant gets its food. Let a few students answer, then separate two ideas on the board: plants take in materials from outside, but they make food inside their leaves. Draw a large leaf and mark sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide as inputs.

Next, trace the journey of each input. Water comes from the soil through roots and stem. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata. Sunlight is trapped by chlorophyll, the green pigment in leaves. Use arrows so students can hear and see the direction of each input.

Finally, write the word equation and read it aloud twice: carbon dioxide plus water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, makes glucose and oxygen. Emphasize that glucose is the plant food, while oxygen is released into the air. Close by asking students to explain why plants are important for animals and humans.
classroomActivity: Give five students cards labelled sunlight, water, carbon dioxide, glucose, and oxygen. Ask the class to arrange them around a plant drawing, then narrate the process in order. Repeat once with students closing their notebooks and using only the cards as prompts.
worksheet: List the three raw materials or conditions needed for photosynthesis.
Explain the role of chlorophyll in one sentence.
Write the word equation for photosynthesis.
Why are leaves called the food factories of the plant?
What happens to the oxygen made during photosynthesis?
A plant is kept in darkness for two days. Predict how this affects food-making and explain why.
answerKey: Water, carbon dioxide, and sunlight are needed; chlorophyll in the leaf is also necessary.
Chlorophyll captures light energy so the leaf can make glucose.
Carbon dioxide + water --sunlight and chlorophyll--> glucose + oxygen.
Leaves are called food factories because they make glucose for the plant.
Oxygen is released into the air through the leaf.
Food-making slows or stops because sunlight is not available as the energy source.
misconceptions: Plants do not get ready-made food from soil; soil provides water and minerals.
Photosynthesis is not the same as breathing; it is food-making.
Only green parts with chlorophyll can photosynthesize strongly.
Oxygen is not an input for photosynthesis; it is an output.

Core: Ask students to explain each arrow and then write the full word equation.
Challenge: Ask students to connect photosynthesis to food chains and oxygen in the air.
screenReaderSummary: Photosynthesis is the food-making process in green plants. Leaves use sunlight, chlorophyll, water from roots, and carbon dioxide from air to make glucose. Oxygen is released from the leaf as a by-product.
audioStudyScript: Listen for the order of the process. Water reaches the leaf from the roots. Carbon dioxide enters through stomata. Chlorophyll traps sunlight. The leaf makes glucose, which is plant food, and oxygen leaves the plant.

title: Plant Nutrition and Stomata
subject: Science
confidenceNotes: Stomata diagram and labels are readable.
Guard-cell label is clear enough for student use.
objective: Students describe autotrophic nutrition and explain how stomata help leaves exchange gases while also losing water vapour.
keyConcepts: Autotrophic nutrition means making food from simple substances using energy.
Plants are autotrophs because they make glucose during photosynthesis.
Stomata are tiny pores mostly found on leaf surfaces.
Guard cells open and close stomata to control gas movement.
Carbon dioxide enters through stomata for photosynthesis.
Oxygen and water vapour can leave through stomata.
Too much water loss through stomata is called transpiration and must be controlled.
teachingScript:
Start with the word autotroph. Break it into auto, meaning self, and troph, meaning nutrition. Explain that plants do not eat like animals; they make food from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight.

Show a simple leaf surface drawing. Mark stomata as tiny doorways. Explain that the plant needs carbon dioxide to enter, but every open doorway can also let water vapour escape. This creates a useful trade-off: open stomata help food-making, but closed stomata reduce water loss.

Use guard cells as the control system. When guard cells swell, the pore opens. When they lose water, the pore closes. End by connecting this topic back to photosynthesis: without stomata, the leaf cannot easily get carbon dioxide.
classroomActivity: Use two students as guard cells standing with arms apart for an open stoma and together for a closed stoma. Other students act as carbon dioxide, oxygen, and water vapour moving in or out only when the stoma is open.

Tiny pores on leaf surfaces.

misconceptions: Stomata are not large holes visible to the naked eye.
Guard cells do not make food; they control the pore.

Plants need gas exchange even though they do not have lungs.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use the doorway acting activity before writing definitions.
Core: Ask students to complete a cause-effect chart for open and closed stomata.
Challenge: Ask students to explain the trade-off between carbon dioxide entry and water conservation.

title: Water Cycle
subject: Science
objective: Students explain the water cycle as the continuous movement of water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection, runoff, and groundwater flow.
keyConcepts: The sun provides energy for evaporation.
Evaporation changes liquid water into water vapour.
Condensation changes water vapour into tiny droplets that form clouds.
Precipitation returns water to Earth as rain, snow, or hail.
Collection gathers water in rivers, lakes, oceans, and underground spaces.
Runoff moves water over land toward rivers and seas.
The cycle repeats, so water is reused in nature.
teachingScript:
Begin with a local rain question: after rain falls near the school, where does the water go? List student answers such as puddles, drains, soil, and rivers. Use these answers to introduce collection and runoff before moving to the full cycle.

Draw the cycle as a loop, not a straight line. Start at a pond or sea. The sun heats water, evaporation sends water vapour upward, condensation forms clouds, precipitation brings water down, and collection gathers it again. Add runoff and groundwater to show that not all water returns by the same path.

Close by asking students why the word cycle is important. They should say that the same water keeps moving and changing form. Connect this to water conservation: even though water cycles, clean usable water is limited.
classroomActivity: Create six floor stations: sun, evaporation, cloud, rain, river, and groundwater. Students move as water drops and announce the process at each station.
worksheet: Define evaporation with an example.
How are clouds formed?
What is precipitation?
Give two places where water collects after rain.

answerKey: Liquid water changes to vapour, such as wet clothes drying.
Water vapour cools and condenses into tiny droplets.
Water falling from clouds as rain, snow, or hail.
Rivers, lakes, oceans, ponds, soil, or groundwater.
The same water moves repeatedly through steps.
It can carry soil away, fill drains, or cause waterlogging.
misconceptions: Clouds are not smoke; they are made of tiny water droplets or ice crystals.
Evaporation can happen even when water is not boiling.
Rain does not mean water has disappeared from clouds forever.
Groundwater is part of the water cycle too.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use numbered process cards and ask students to arrange them in a circle.
Core: Ask students to explain each stage using a local monsoon example.
Challenge: Ask students to include runoff and groundwater in a more complete cycle diagram.
screenReaderSummary: The water cycle is the continuous movement of water between Earth and the air. The sun causes evaporation, cooling causes condensation, clouds release precipitation, and water collects in oceans, rivers, lakes, soil, and underground spaces.
audioStudyScript: Imagine one drop of water. The sun warms it and it evaporates. It rises as vapour, cools, and becomes part of a cloud. Later it falls as rain. It may collect in a river, soak into the ground, or flow back to the sea. Then the journey begins again.

title: Cloud Formation and Rainfall
subject: Science
objective: Students explain how water vapour cools to form clouds and why droplets eventually fall as rain.
keyConcepts: Warm air can hold water vapour and often rises.
Air becomes cooler as it rises higher.
Cooling water vapour condenses into tiny droplets.
Millions of tiny droplets together form clouds.
Droplets join to become larger and heavier.
When droplets become too heavy to stay in the cloud, they fall as rain.
Rainfall can be affected by wind, temperature, and landforms.
teachingScript:
Start by asking students why bathroom mirrors become foggy after hot water is used. Use this familiar example to introduce condensation: warm water vapour touches a cooler surface and becomes tiny drops.

Now move from the mirror to the sky. Warm moist air rises. Higher air is cooler, so water vapour condenses around dust particles into tiny droplets. These droplets are small enough to float as clouds.

Explain rainfall as a size and weight change. Droplets collide and join. When they become heavy, gravity pulls them down as rain. Connect this to dark clouds before rain: more droplets make the cloud thicker and less light passes through.
classroomActivity: Hold a cold steel plate over a cup of warm water for a short teacher demonstration. Let students observe droplets forming on the plate and connect the model to cloud formation.
worksheet: Why does warm moist air rise?
What happens when water vapour cools?
How do tiny droplets become rain?
Why may rain clouds look dark?
Give one everyday example of condensation.
How is this topic part of the water cycle?
answerKey: Warm air is lighter and rises.
It condenses into tiny water droplets.
Droplets join, become heavy, and fall.
Many droplets block more light.
Foggy mirror or drops on a cold bottle.
Cloud formation is condensation and rainfall is precipitation.
misconceptions: Clouds are not made of smoke or cotton.
Rain does not fall because clouds melt.
Condensation can happen without boiling.
Dark clouds are not dirty; they often contain many droplets.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use the mirror or cold-bottle example before using weather words.
Core: Ask students to sequence warm air, cooling, condensation, cloud, rainfall.
Challenge: Ask students to compare cloud formation with dew on grass or droplets on a cold bottle.
screenReaderSummary: Clouds form when warm moist air rises and cools. Water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. When droplets join and become heavy, they fall to Earth as rain.
audioStudyScript: Warm moist air rises. Higher up, the air is cooler. Water vapour changes into tiny drops. The drops gather as clouds. When many drops join and become heavy, rain falls.

stepByStepExplanation: First, water evaporates and adds vapour to air. Second, warm moist air rises. Third, the air cools. Fourth, vapour condenses into droplets. Fifth, droplets form clouds. Sixth, droplets join and fall as rainfall.

title: Digestive System Overview
subject: Science
objective: Students trace the path of food through the digestive system and state the main role of each organ.
keyConcepts: Digestion breaks complex food into simpler usable substances.
The mouth starts mechanical digestion by chewing.
Saliva begins chemical digestion of starch.
The oesophagus pushes food to the stomach.
The stomach churns food and mixes it with digestive juices.
The small intestine completes digestion and absorbs most nutrients.
The large intestine absorbs water and forms waste for removal.
teachingScript:
Begin by asking students to imagine eating a piece of roti or rice. Ask: where does it go first, and does it remain the same? Use this question to introduce digestion as both a physical and chemical process.

Draw the digestive tract as one continuous route. Move slowly from mouth to anus. At each stop, give one short job: mouth chews, oesophagus pushes, stomach churns, small intestine absorbs nutrients, large intestine absorbs water, anus removes waste.

Emphasize that the digestive system is not a bag of separate organs. It is a connected tube with helper organs and juices. End with a quick oral recap where students say the organs in order without looking.
classroomActivity: Use a long rope or chalk path as the digestive tract. Students hold organ cards in order and pass a food card along the path, announcing each organ job.
worksheet: Write the organs of the digestive tract in order.

What does the oesophagus do?
Why is the small intestine important?
What does the large intestine absorb?
Why should we chew food well?
answerKey: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus.
Chewing breaks food physically; chemical digestion uses juices to change food.
It pushes food to the stomach.
It absorbs most nutrients.
Water.
Chewing makes food smaller and mixes it with saliva.
misconceptions: Food does not pass into the lungs during normal swallowing.
The stomach does not absorb most nutrients.
Digestion is not only chewing; chemical digestion also occurs.
The intestines are not just waste pipes; they absorb useful materials.
differentiatedSupport:

Challenge: Ask students to compare mechanical and chemical digestion with examples.
screenReaderSummary: The digestive system is a connected path that breaks food into simpler substances. Food moves from mouth to oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and anus. Nutrients are mostly absorbed in the small intestine.
audioStudyScript: Food starts in the mouth. Teeth break it into smaller pieces and saliva begins digestion. The oesophagus pushes food down. The stomach churns it. The small intestine absorbs nutrients. The large intestine absorbs water and waste leaves the body.

Step 5: The small intestine absorbs nutrients. Step 6: The large intestine absorbs water. Step 7: Waste is removed.

title: Teeth, Saliva, and Enzymes
subject: Science
objective: Students explain how teeth, tongue, saliva, and enzymes begin digestion in the mouth.
keyConcepts: Digestion begins in the mouth, not the stomach.
Different teeth have different shapes and jobs.
Incisors cut food and canines tear food.
Premolars and molars crush and grind food.
Saliva moistens food and helps form a soft bolus.
The enzyme amylase begins digestion of starch.
The tongue helps mix food with saliva and pushes it for swallowing.
teachingScript:
Start by asking students to eat one imaginary bite slowly. What happens before swallowing? List cutting, grinding, wetting, mixing, tasting, and pushing. Use this list to show that the mouth is an active digestive organ.

Draw four tooth types and connect shape to function. Incisors are sharp like a cutter. Canines are pointed for tearing. Molars are broad for grinding. Students should understand that structure helps function.

Then introduce saliva. It is not just water; it moistens food and contains amylase, an enzyme that begins breaking down starch. Keep the enzyme explanation simple: enzymes are helpers that speed up digestion. Link this to why chewing well makes digestion easier.
classroomActivity: Give students food-job cards such as cut, tear, grind, moisten, mix, and swallow. They match each job to incisors, canines, molars, saliva, or tongue.
worksheet: Name two types of teeth and their jobs.

What is an enzyme?

Why is chewing food properly important?
answerKey: Incisors cut, canines tear, molars grind.
A liquid in the mouth that moistens food and contains enzymes.
It mixes food and helps push it for swallowing.
A substance that helps speed up chemical digestion.
Amylase.
It makes food smaller and mixes it with saliva.
misconceptions: Saliva is not useless water; it helps digestion.
All teeth do not have the same job.

differentiatedSupport:

Challenge: Ask students to predict what happens if food is swallowed without chewing well.

title: Acids, Bases, and Indicators
subject: Science
confidenceNotes: One sample label needs teacher confirmation.
objective: Students classify common substances as acidic, basic, or neutral using safe indicator tests.
keyConcepts: Acids and bases are groups of substances with different properties.
Many acids taste sour, but tasting unknown substances is unsafe and not allowed.
Many bases feel slippery, but touching unknown substances is unsafe.
Indicators change colour to show whether a substance is acidic or basic.
Blue litmus turns red in an acid.
Red litmus turns blue in a base.
Neutral substances do not show acid or base colour changes with litmus.
teachingScript:
Begin with familiar safe examples: lemon juice, curd, soap solution, and baking soda solution. Make it very clear that students should not taste or touch unknown samples in a lab. Safety comes before testing.

Introduce litmus as an indicator. Demonstrate the two key rules slowly: acids turn blue litmus red, bases turn red litmus blue. Put these two rules in a small table and have students read it aloud.

Then show how to record observations. A good observation table includes sample name, red litmus result, blue litmus result, and conclusion. Close by asking why indicators are better than guessing from smell or taste.
classroomActivity: Use coloured paper strips as pretend litmus. Call out safe examples and ask students to hold up the expected colour-change card before revealing the answer.
worksheet: What is an indicator?
What happens to blue litmus in an acid?
What happens to red litmus in a base?
Why should unknown substances not be tasted?
Classify lemon juice, soap solution, and pure water using litmus rules.
Design a four-column observation table for a litmus test.

It turns red.
It turns blue.
It may be harmful or corrosive.

misconceptions: Students must not identify acids by tasting in class.

Challenge: Ask students to explain why safety rules are part of scientific method.

audioStudyScript: Remember two litmus rules. Acid changes blue litmus to red. Base changes red litmus to blue. If there is no acid or base change, the sample may be neutral. Always test safely.

title: Natural Indicators
subject: Science
sourceType: Turmeric and China rose activity notes
confidenceNotes: Colour-change table needs teacher colour check.
objective: Students explain how natural indicators such as turmeric and China rose can show acidic or basic nature through colour changes.
keyConcepts: Indicators can be made from some natural materials.
Turmeric remains yellow in acids but turns reddish-brown in bases.
China rose extract shows different colours in acids and bases.
Natural indicators are useful for simple school demonstrations.

teachingScript:
Begin by connecting to litmus: litmus is one indicator, but not the only one. Ask students if kitchen materials can help in science. Introduce turmeric as a familiar material that changes colour with bases.

Explain the turmeric paper test. A turmeric strip is yellow. If a basic solution such as soap water touches it, the strip becomes reddish-brown. Acidic lemon juice does not create the same change. Students should compare with an unused strip.

Then introduce China rose as another natural indicator. Emphasize careful observation: colour words should be written immediately, and the sample must be labelled. End by discussing why natural indicators are useful but less precise than laboratory indicators.
classroomActivity: Prepare paper cards coloured yellow and reddish-brown. Students classify pretend samples and place them in acid/base/neutral columns based on the indicator result.
worksheet: What is a natural indicator?
What colour change does turmeric show in a base?
Why should we use labelled safe samples?
How does a control strip help?
Name two natural indicators.

To avoid unsafe unknown chemicals.
It lets us compare the original colour.
Turmeric and China rose.

Turmeric does not turn the same colour for every substance.
A faint colour change should be compared with a control.

audioStudyScript: A natural indicator works like a colour signal. Turmeric is yellow. In a base like soap solution, turmeric can turn reddish-brown. Use a control strip and record the colour carefully.

title: Fractions on a Number Line
subject: Math
objective: Students place proper fractions between 0 and 1 on a number line by dividing the whole into equal intervals.
keyConcepts: A number line shows numbers in order from left to right.
The interval from 0 to 1 represents one whole.
The denominator tells how many equal parts the whole is divided into.
The numerator tells how many parts to count from 0.
Fractions must be placed on spaces, not by counting tick marks incorrectly.
Equal spacing is necessary for accurate placement.
Number lines help compare fractions by position.
teachingScript:
Draw a large line from 0 to 1. Ask students what the whole is. Explain that the whole is the full distance from 0 to 1, not just the marks.

For fourths, divide the distance into four equal spaces. Count spaces aloud: one-fourth, two-fourths, three-fourths, four-fourths. Mark one-half at two-fourths and show that it is exactly midway.

Then address the common mistake: students often count tick marks instead of spaces. Circle the spaces and have the class count them. Close by comparing one-fourth, one-half, and three-fourths by their positions from left to right.
classroomActivity: Use floor tape as a number line from 0 to 1. Four students hold interval cards and stand at one-fourth, one-half, three-fourths, and one whole.
worksheet: Draw a number line from 0 to 1 and mark one-half.
Mark one-fourth and three-fourths.
Explain why spaces must be equal.
Which is larger: one-half or one-fourth?
Show that two-fourths and one-half are at the same point.
Write a mistake someone might make when marking thirds.
answerKey: One-half is midway between 0 and 1.
One-fourth is after the first of four equal spaces; three-fourths after the third.
Unequal spaces give wrong values.
One-half.
Both are at the middle point.
Counting tick marks instead of spaces is a common mistake.
misconceptions: A larger denominator does not automatically mean a larger fraction.
Tick marks and spaces are not the same thing.
One-half is not always drawn larger; its position shows its value.
Fractions on number lines need equal intervals.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Count spaces aloud and use colour for each equal interval.
Core: Ask students to place halves, fourths, and thirds and explain the denominator.
Challenge: Ask students to prove equivalent positions such as one-half and two-fourths.
screenReaderSummary: A fraction can be placed on a number line by dividing the distance from 0 to 1 into equal spaces. The denominator tells the number of spaces, and the numerator tells how many spaces to count from 0.
audioStudyScript: Start at zero. The whole distance to one is one whole. If the denominator is four, split the distance into four equal spaces. To mark three-fourths, count three spaces from zero.
visualDescription: The worksheet shows a horizontal number line from 0 to 1 divided into four equal parts with labels one-fourth, one-half, and three-fourths.
stepByStepExplanation: Step 1: Draw 0 and 1. Step 2: Read the denominator. Step 3: Split the whole into that many equal spaces. Step 4: Read the numerator. Step 5: Count that many spaces from 0. Step 6: Mark the fraction point.

vocabulary.meaning: Top number showing counted parts.
Bottom number showing equal parts in the whole.
Space between two marks on a number line.
A fraction less than 1.
Fractions that have the same value.

practiceQuestions: How many equal spaces are needed for fifths?
Where is one-half on a number line?
Why is two-fourths equal to one-half?
Which is greater: three-fourths or one-fourth?
What mistake happens if you count tick marks?
Place two-thirds in words.
selfCheckAnswers: They are at the same point.
You may mark the wrong position.
Divide into three equal spaces and count two from 0.

title: Equivalent Fractions
subject: Math
objective: Students identify and create equivalent fractions using visual models and multiplication or division of numerator and denominator.
keyConcepts: Equivalent fractions represent the same value.
Different numerators and denominators can name the same amount.
Multiplying numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number creates an equivalent fraction.
Dividing numerator and denominator by the same common factor simplifies a fraction.
Fraction strips can show equivalence visually.
Equivalent fractions occupy the same point on a number line.
Simplest form has no common factor except 1.
teachingScript:
Start with fraction strips: shade one-half, two-fourths, and four-eighths using strips of the same length. Ask students what they notice. Guide them to say the shaded length is the same even though the numbers are different.

Then move to the rule. If the numerator and denominator are both multiplied by the same number, the size of the fraction does not change because the whole is split into smaller equal parts and more parts are counted.

Finally, reverse the process to simplify. Show four-eighths divided by 4 over 4 to get one-half. Make students say: whatever I do to the numerator, I must do to the denominator.
classroomActivity: Give groups paper strips folded into halves, fourths, and eighths. They shade matching amounts and write all equivalent fraction names they can see.
worksheet: Write two fractions equivalent to one-half.
Simplify 6/9.
Explain using a diagram why 2/4 equals 1/2.
Which is not equivalent to 3/4: 6/8, 9/12, 4/5?
Create an equivalent fraction for 5/6 with denominator 18.
answerKey: Examples: 2/4 and 4/8.
Both cover the same amount of the same whole.
misconceptions: Changing only the numerator changes the value.
Equivalent fractions are not always visually larger because numbers are larger.
Simplest form does not mean smallest numerator only.
The same whole must be used when comparing fraction diagrams.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use fraction strips before symbolic rules.
Core: Ask students to generate equivalents with multiplication and check visually.
Challenge: Ask students to explain equivalence using both number line and fraction strip models.
screenReaderSummary: Equivalent fractions have the same value even when their numbers look different. Multiplying or dividing the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number keeps the fraction equivalent.
audioStudyScript: One-half, two-fourths, and four-eighths can all show the same amount. The rule is simple: multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number. The value stays the same.
visualDescription: Fraction strips of equal length show one-half, two-fourths, and four-eighths shaded to the same length.
stepByStepExplanation: Step 1: Start with a fraction. Step 2: Choose the same multiplier for top and bottom. Step 3: Multiply numerator. Step 4: Multiply denominator. Step 5: Compare with a visual or number line. Step 6: To simplify, divide top and bottom by a common factor.

vocabulary.meaning: Fractions with the same value.
Write a fraction in a smaller equivalent form.
A number that divides both numerator and denominator.
A visual strip used to compare fractions.
A fraction with no common factor except 1.

steps: Make or find equal shaded amount.
Multiply top and bottom by same number.
Divide top and bottom by same factor to simplify.
practiceQuestions: Why is 2/4 equivalent to 1/2?
Find an equivalent fraction for 2/3 with denominator 12.
Simplify 8/12.
Which rule keeps the fraction value same?
What is simplest form?
Show 3/6 on a number line and name its simpler form.
selfCheckAnswers: Multiply or divide numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number.
It is at one-half, so simpler form is 1/2.
homework: Make a table of five fractions and two equivalent fractions for each.

title: Linear Equations
subject: Math
confidenceNotes: Main equation and answer are readable.
One intermediate line needs teacher review.
objective: Students solve one-step and two-step linear equations by applying inverse operations equally to both sides.
keyConcepts: An equation says two expressions are equal.
A variable represents an unknown number.
Solving means finding the value that makes the equation true.
Both sides must stay balanced after every operation.
Inverse operations undo each other.
For two-step equations, remove addition or subtraction before multiplication or division.
Checking the answer confirms that the solution is correct.
teachingScript:
Begin with a balance idea. If two sides are equal and we remove the same weight from both sides, they remain equal. Connect this physical image to equations: whatever operation we do to one side, we must do to the other.

Solve 2x + 3 = 7 slowly. First subtract 3 from both sides to isolate 2x. Then divide both sides by 2 to isolate x. Write every line vertically so students can see the equation changing step by step.

Finish with checking. Substitute x = 2 into the original equation: 2 times 2 plus 3 equals 7. Because the left side becomes 7 and the right side is 7, the solution is correct.
classroomActivity: Draw a balance scale on the board. Students suggest the same operation for both pans while solving equations written on sticky notes.
worksheet: Solve x + 5 = 12.
Solve 3x = 18.
Solve 2x + 3 = 11.
Solve 5x - 4 = 16.
Check whether x = 3 solves 4x + 1 = 13.
Explain why doing an operation on only one side is wrong.
answerKey: Yes, because 4(3)+1=13.
It breaks equality and makes the equation unbalanced.
misconceptions: Students may change only one side of the equation.
Students may divide before removing the added constant.
The check must use the original equation, not only the last line.
The variable is not always x; any letter can represent the unknown.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use bilingual operation words: add/jodo, subtract/ghatao, divide/bhaag.
Core: Ask students to write one operation per line and say why equality remains true.
Challenge: Ask students to create an equation for a partner and include a check step.
screenReaderSummary: A linear equation can be solved by keeping both sides balanced. Use inverse operations to isolate the variable, then substitute the answer into the original equation to check it.
audioStudyScript: For 2x plus 3 equals 7, first subtract 3 from both sides. Now 2x equals 4. Divide both sides by 2. x equals 2. Check in the original equation.
visualDescription: The worksheet shows a balance-scale sketch next to the equation 2x plus 3 equals 7 and a vertical worked solution.
stepByStepExplanation: Step 1: Identify the variable term. Step 2: Undo addition or subtraction on both sides. Step 3: Undo multiplication or division on both sides. Step 4: Write the variable value. Step 5: Substitute it into the original equation. Step 6: Confirm both sides match.

vocabulary.meaning: A statement that two expressions are equal.
A symbol for an unknown number.
An operation that undoes another operation.
A value that makes an equation true.
Substituting the answer to verify it works.

steps: Write the value of the variable.
practiceQuestions: Why must both sides get the same operation?
Solve x - 4 = 9.
Solve 4x = 20.
Solve 3x + 2 = 14.
How do you check x = 4 for 3x + 2 = 14?
What is an inverse operation?
homework: Solve five two-step equations and show the check for two of them.
localLanguageSupport: Hindi support: dono taraf same operation karo; pehle plus/minus hatao, phir multiply/divide hatao.
warnings: Low lighting may affect OCR accuracy.

title: Word Problems to Equations
subject: Math
objective: Students translate simple word problems into linear equations and solve them using a defined variable.
keyConcepts: A word problem must be read for meaning before solving.
The unknown quantity should be named with a variable.
Words such as increased by, more than, total, and times suggest operations.
The phrase is or equals usually tells where the equal sign belongs.
A sentence can become an equation when relationships are written mathematically.
The solution must answer the original question, not only give x.
Checking in words helps confirm that the answer makes sense.
teachingScript:
Start with a short sentence: A number increased by 5 is 17. Ask students what is unknown. Write: let the number be x. Underline increased by 5 and translate it to x + 5. Underline is 17 and write equals 17.

Solve the equation only after the translation is clear. x + 5 = 17 gives x = 12. Then read the original sentence again: 12 increased by 5 is 17. This checks both the equation and the answer.

Repeat with multiplication language such as three times a number is 24. Emphasize that students should not rush to calculate before defining the variable and writing the equation.
classroomActivity: Students work in pairs with sentence cards. One partner underlines operation words, the other writes the equation. They swap cards and check each other.
worksheet: Translate: A number increased by 6 is 20.
Translate: Four times a number is 28.
Solve: x + 6 = 20.
Solve: 4x = 28.
A number decreased by 3 is 15. Write and solve.
The cost of 3 notebooks is Rs 45. Write an equation for one notebook cost and solve.
misconceptions: Students may write numbers in the order they appear without reading meaning.
Times means multiplication, not addition.
The answer should include what the variable represents.
Some phrases need careful reading, especially decreased by and less than.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use a three-column table: words, operation, equation.
Core: Ask students to define x and underline operation phrases before solving.
Challenge: Ask students to write their own word problem for a given equation.
screenReaderSummary: To solve a word problem with equations, first decide what is unknown and name it with a variable. Then translate operation words into symbols, write an equation, solve it, and check the answer in the original sentence.
audioStudyScript: Read the sentence slowly. Ask: what is unknown? Let it be x. Translate the words into maths. Increased by means plus. Times means multiply. Is means equals. Then solve and check in the sentence.
visualDescription: The worksheet has a table with word phrases on the left, operation symbols in the middle, and equations on the right.
stepByStepExplanation: Step 1: Read the full problem. Step 2: Choose the unknown. Step 3: Write let the unknown be x. Step 4: Underline operation words. Step 5: Write the equation. Step 6: Solve. Step 7: Answer in words and check.

vocabulary.meaning: Change words into mathematical symbols.
A letter for an unknown amount.
A phrase often meaning addition.
A phrase meaning multiplication.
A mathematical sentence with an equal sign.

practiceQuestions: What should you do before writing an equation?
Translate: a number plus 9 is 30.
Translate: five times a number is 40.
Solve x - 8 = 12.
Why should the answer be checked in words?
Write a word problem for 2x + 3 = 15.
selfCheckAnswers: To ensure it answers the original question.
Example: Twice a number plus 3 is 15.
homework: Write three word problems from daily life and solve them using equations.

title: Area and Perimeter of Rectangles
subject: Math
objective: Students distinguish area from perimeter and calculate both for rectangles using correct units.
keyConcepts: Area measures the space covered inside a closed shape.
Perimeter measures the total distance around a closed shape.
Rectangle area is length multiplied by breadth.
Rectangle perimeter is 2 times the sum of length and breadth.
Area uses square units because it counts unit squares.
Perimeter uses linear units because it measures boundary length.
The same rectangle has both area and perimeter, but they answer different questions.
teachingScript:
Hold up a notebook. Ask students to point to the inside cover and then trace the outside edge. Name the inside measure area and the outside boundary measure perimeter. This physical contrast helps prevent formula mixing.

Draw a rectangle labelled 8 cm and 5 cm. For area, shade the inside and explain that we are counting square centimetres. Calculate 8 x 5 = 40 square cm. For perimeter, trace the border and add all sides or use 2(l+b): 2(8+5)=26 cm.

End with unit checking. If the answer describes covered space, it needs square units. If it describes distance around, it needs cm, m, or another length unit.
classroomActivity: Students measure a rectangular notebook, desk tile, or paper sheet. They calculate area and perimeter, then explain which result needs square units.
worksheet: Find the area of a rectangle 8 cm by 5 cm.
Find the perimeter of the same rectangle.
A rectangle is 12 m long and 4 m wide. Find its area.
Find its perimeter.
Which measure would you use for painting a wall?
Which measure would you use for fencing a garden?
answerKey: 40 square cm.
26 cm.
48 square m.
Area.
Perimeter.
misconceptions: Area and perimeter are not interchangeable.
Perimeter does not use square units.
Area is not found by adding all sides.
A larger perimeter does not always mean a larger area without checking dimensions.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Colour the inside for area and outline the boundary for perimeter.
Core: Ask students to solve two examples and explain units aloud.
Challenge: Ask students to compare rectangles with same perimeter but different areas.
screenReaderSummary: Area is the amount of space inside a rectangle. Perimeter is the distance around it. Area of a rectangle is length times breadth and uses square units. Perimeter is the sum of all sides and uses length units.
audioStudyScript: For area, think inside the rectangle. Multiply length by breadth. For perimeter, think around the rectangle. Add all four sides, or use two times length plus breadth. Always check the unit.
visualDescription: The notes show a rectangle labelled 8 cm by 5 cm. The inside is shaded for area and the border is highlighted for perimeter.
stepByStepExplanation: Step 1: Identify length and breadth. Step 2: Decide whether the question asks inside space or boundary distance. Step 3: For area, multiply length by breadth. Step 4: For perimeter, add all sides or use 2(l+b). Step 5: Write square units for area and length units for perimeter.

vocabulary.meaning: Space inside a closed shape.
Distance around a closed shape.
Longer side of a rectangle.
Shorter side or width of a rectangle.
A unit used to measure area.

practiceQuestions: What does area measure?
What does perimeter measure?
Find area of 10 cm by 6 cm.
Find perimeter of 10 cm by 6 cm.
Why does area use square units?
Give a real-life use of perimeter.
homework: Measure one rectangular object at home and find both area and perimeter.

title: Composite Rectangles
subject: Math
equations: Total area = Area A + Area B
confidenceNotes: A small side label should be verified.
objective: Students find the area of composite rectilinear shapes by splitting them into rectangles and adding the parts.
keyConcepts: A composite shape is made from two or more simple shapes.
An L-shaped rectilinear figure can be split into rectangles.
Each rectangle area is found using length times breadth.
The total area is the sum of the non-overlapping parts.
A missing side can often be found by subtracting known lengths.
A clear split line prevents double-counting or missing a part.
Units remain square units for total area.
teachingScript:
Show an L-shaped figure and ask why the simple rectangle formula cannot be used on the full outline directly. Guide students to see that the shape is not one complete rectangle.

Draw a dashed line that splits the L-shape into two rectangles. Label them A and B. Calculate each area separately and write the results in a small table. Add the two areas only after checking that the rectangles do not overlap.

Discuss missing sides. If the total length is 10 cm and one part is 4 cm, the missing part is 6 cm. Students should find missing lengths before calculating area. Close with a warning: do not add all side lengths when the question asks area.
classroomActivity: Give groups grid-paper L-shapes. Students draw one split line, label rectangles, count grid squares to estimate area, then use multiplication to confirm.
worksheet: What is a composite shape?
Split an L-shape into two rectangles and label them A and B.
Rectangle A is 8 cm by 3 cm. Find its area.
Rectangle B is 4 cm by 5 cm. Find its area.
Find the total area from A and B.
If a total side is 12 cm and one part is 7 cm, find the missing part.
answerKey: A shape made from simpler shapes.
Any correct non-overlapping split is acceptable.
24 square cm.
20 square cm.
44 square cm.
5 cm.
misconceptions: Adding all boundary sides gives perimeter, not area.
Overlapping rectangles should not both be counted.
A missing side is not guessed; it is calculated from known lengths.
The split line should create simple rectangles.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use grid paper and tactile tracing of the two rectangles.
Core: Ask students to complete an area table before adding.
Challenge: Ask students to solve the same shape using two different splits and compare totals.
screenReaderSummary: Composite rectangles are shapes made from more than one rectangle. To find area, split the shape into non-overlapping rectangles, calculate each rectangle area, and add the areas together.
audioStudyScript: Do not try one formula for the whole L-shape. Split it into rectangles. Find area A. Find area B. Add them. If a side is missing, subtract known lengths first.
visualDescription: The worksheet shows an L-shaped figure with a dashed line dividing it into two labelled rectangles. A side-length table is written beside the shape.
stepByStepExplanation: Step 1: Look for a way to split the shape into rectangles. Step 2: Draw a dashed split line. Step 3: Find any missing side lengths. Step 4: Calculate each rectangle area. Step 5: Add the areas. Step 6: Write the answer in square units.

vocabulary.meaning: A shape made of two or more simpler shapes.
Made from straight horizontal and vertical sides.
A helper line used to divide a shape.
Sum of all non-overlapping part areas.
A side length that must be calculated from given lengths.

practiceQuestions: Why split a composite shape?

title: Reading Bar Graphs
subject: Math
objective: Students read and interpret bar graphs using title, axes, scale, labels, and bar heights.
keyConcepts: A bar graph compares quantities across categories.
The title tells what data is shown.
The x-axis usually lists categories.
The y-axis shows numbers or frequency.
The scale tells the value of each step.
Bar height represents the quantity for a category.
Correct comparison requires reading the scale carefully.
teachingScript:
Show the graph without asking calculation questions first. Ask students to identify the title, x-axis, y-axis, and scale. This builds graph-reading habits before answers.

Next, choose one bar and model how to read its value. Start at the category label, move up to the top of the bar, then across to the y-axis scale. Remind students that each square may represent more than one item.

Finally, ask comparison questions: tallest bar, shortest bar, difference between two bars, and total for selected categories. Close by asking students to write one sentence conclusion from the graph.
classroomActivity: Students vote for a favourite fruit or game. Build a live bar graph using sticky notes, then ask students to read values and comparisons.
worksheet: What does the graph title tell us?
Which axis has category names?
What does the scale mean?
Which bar is tallest?
How do you find the difference between two bars?
Write one conclusion from the graph.
answerKey: It tells the topic of the data.
The x-axis.
The value of each step or box.
The bar with the greatest height.
Read both values and subtract.
Any accurate conclusion based on the data.
misconceptions: Students may ignore the scale and count boxes as 1 each.
The tallest bar must still be read using the y-axis.
A graph conclusion should come from data, not personal opinion.
Different graphs can use different scales.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use finger tracking from category to bar top to scale.
Core: Ask students to answer value, comparison, and conclusion questions.
Challenge: Ask students to critique whether a graph scale is easy or misleading.

audioStudyScript: First read the title. Then read the x-axis categories and y-axis scale. Pick a bar, go to its top, and read the value from the scale. Use values to compare bars.
visualDescription: The worksheet shows a bar graph about favourite fruits with mango, banana, and apple on the x-axis and number of students on the y-axis.
stepByStepExplanation: Step 1: Read the title. Step 2: Read both axes. Step 3: Check the scale. Step 4: Find the category. Step 5: Read the bar height. Step 6: Compare or calculate using the values. Step 7: Write a data-based conclusion.

vocabulary.meaning: A graph that uses bars to compare categories.
The value represented by each step on an axis.
A reference line on a graph.
A group being compared.
How many times something occurs.

practiceQuestions: Why should you read the title first?
What does the y-axis show?
What does scale mean?
How do you find the tallest category?
How do you find the difference between two bars?

title: Mean, Median, and Mode
subject: Math
equations: Mean = sum of values / number of values
confidenceNotes: Formula and data set are readable.
objective: Students calculate mean, median, and mode for a small data set and explain what each measure tells about the data.
keyConcepts: Data are collected values or observations.
Mean is the arithmetic average found by total divided by count.
Median is the middle value after data are arranged in order.
Mode is the value that occurs most often.
A data set can have no mode or more than one mode.
Mean is affected by very large or very small values.
Choosing a measure depends on what question we want to answer.
teachingScript:
Start with a small familiar data set: marks of five students or number of books read. Write the numbers clearly and ask what one number could represent the group. Introduce mean, median, and mode as three different summary measures.

For mean, add all values and divide by the number of values. For median, arrange values in order and find the middle. For mode, look for the value that repeats most. Work the same data set through all three measures so students can compare them.

Discuss meaning, not only calculation. Mean balances the total equally. Median shows the middle position. Mode shows the most common value. Use a data set with an unusually high value to show why mean can change a lot.
classroomActivity: Collect the number of siblings or books read by students in one row. Calculate mean, median, and mode together, then ask which measure best describes the row.
worksheet: Find the mean of 4, 6, 6, 8, 10.
Find the median of 4, 6, 6, 8, 10.
Find the mode of 4, 6, 6, 8, 10.
Why must data be ordered before finding median?
Find the mode of 2, 3, 4, 5.
Which measure is most affected by one very large value?
answerKey: The middle value depends on order.
No mode.
Mean.
misconceptions: Median is not found by adding and dividing.
Mode is not always the largest number.
Data must be ordered before finding median.
Mean can be a decimal even when all data values are whole numbers.
differentiatedSupport:
Support: Use three labelled boxes: average, middle, most common.
Core: Ask students to calculate all three for the same ordered data set.
Challenge: Ask students to decide which measure is best for a data story with an outlier.
screenReaderSummary: Mean, median, and mode are three ways to summarize data. Mean is total divided by count. Median is the middle value after ordering. Mode is the value that appears most often.
audioStudyScript: Mean means share the total equally. Median means middle after ordering. Mode means most often. Use the same data set and calculate each one carefully.
visualDescription: The notes show a data list in order, a circled middle value for median, a repeated value for mode, and a formula box for mean.
stepByStepExplanation: Step 1: Write the data set. Step 2: For mean, add all values and divide by count. Step 3: For median, order values and find the middle. Step 4: For mode, find the most repeated value. Step 5: Write what each measure means in the context.

vocabulary.meaning: Collected values or observations.
Average found by total divided by count.
Middle value after ordering.
Most frequent value.
A value very different from the others.

practiceQuestions: Find mean of 2, 4, 6.
Find median of 7, 3, 5.
Find mode of 1, 2, 2, 3, 4.
Can a data set have no mode?
Which measure uses all values?
Why can an outlier affect mean?
selfCheckAnswers: It changes the total before division.
homework: Collect five numbers from a small survey and calculate mean, median, and mode.
